subject: Uniform+VonMises mixture model working! But slowly...

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Uniform+VonMises mixture model working! But slowly...
parts:
Hi folks,

I finally got around to making use of the von_mises distribution that was added recently, and I was able to code up a working example of a hierarchical mixture (uniform+von_mises) model for circular data: 

https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/10298188

However, I'm finding it slow to evaluate, yielding only 1000-2000 effective samples after a day of crunching on a relatively fast machine. While this is ok for now, I was hoping on increasing the complexity to the model, including adding parameters to evaluate correlations across levels of my random effect amongst the existing parameters. Any advice on tweaks I might apply to make the code more efficient?

Oh, and in case this is related, I'm getting really strong autocorrelation in the samples for most of the parameters, even with chains of length 1e5. There's also pretty strong crosscorrelation between a few pairs of parameters.

Thoughts?

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

On Wed, Apr 9, 2014 at 2:12 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi folks,

I finally got around to making use of the von_mises distribution that was added recently, and I was able to code up a working example of a hierarchical mixture (uniform+von_mises) model for circular data: 

https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/10298188

However, I'm finding it slow to evaluate, yielding only 1000-2000 effective samples after a day of crunching on a relatively fast machine. While this is ok for now, I was hoping on increasing the complexity to the model, including adding parameters to evaluate correlations across levels of my random effect amongst the existing parameters. Any advice on tweaks I might apply to make the code more efficient?

Oh, and in case this is related, I'm getting really strong autocorrelation in the samples for most of the parameters, even with chains of length 1e5. There's also pretty strong crosscorrelation between a few pairs of parameters.

Thoughts?

Well, for one you can vectorize things a bit more.  Instead of:

//define sampling of unit-specific parameters
for (n in 1:N){
logitRho[n] ~ normal(logitRhoMean,logitRhoSD);
logKappa[n] ~ normal(logKappaMean,logKappaSD);
logitRhoEffect[n] ~ normal(logitRhoEffectMean,logitRhoEffectSD);
logKappaEffect[n] ~ normal(logKappaEffectMean,logKappaEffectSD);
}

just do

logitRho ~ normal(logitRhoMean,logitRhoSD);
logKappa ~ normal(logKappaMean,logKappaSD);
logitRhoEffect ~ normal(logitRhoEffectMean,logitRhoEffectSD);
logKappaEffect ~ normal(logKappaEffectMean,logKappaEffectSD);

This will help a little, depending on how large N is.

Also, you should be able to compute log(rho[]) directly from logitRho.

Finally, if 2*N << L, then it might be worth precomputing values and just indexing them when looping over L.

Those things should help speed up the model, but won't necessarily help with convergence issues and strong autocorrelations.

Cheers,
Marcus

--

Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

Thanks truly,

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Uniform+VonMises mixture model working! But slowly...
parts:
Ok, I actually just realized that my idea probably wouldn't work as well as I'd thought but here it is.

In transformed data:

real neglog2pi;
neglog2pi <- -log(2.0 * pi());

and in transformed parameters:

vector[N] logrho[2];
vector[N] log1mrho_neglog2pi[2];
for (n in 1:N) {

// compute rho and kappa here then...
  logrho[n,1] <- log(rho[n,1]);
  logrho[n,2] <- log(rho[n,2]);
  log1mrho_neglog2pi[n,1] <- log1m(rho[n,1]) + neglog2pi;
  log1mrho_neglog2pi[n,2] <- log1m(rho[n,2]) + neglog2pi;
}

then in model:

ps[1] <- logrho[unit[i],conditions[i]] + ...

ps[2] <- log1mrho_neglog2pi[unit[i],condition[i]];

This should shave some more time off so long as 2*N << L.

Cheers,
Marcus

  logrho[n,2] <- log(rho[n,2]);
  log1mrho_neglog2pi[n,1] <- log1m(rho[n,1]) + neglog2pi;
  log1mrho_neglog2pi[n,2] <- log1m(rho[n,2]) + neglog2pi;
}

then in model:

ps[1] <- logrho[unit[i],conditions[i]] + ...

ps[2] <- log1mrho_neglog2pi[unit[i],condition[i]];

This should shave some more time off so long as 2*N << L.

Cheers,
Marcus

Hi folks,

I finally got around to making use of the von_mises distribution that was added recently, and I was able to code up a working example of a hierarchical mixture (uniform+von_mises) model for circular data: 

https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/10298188

However, I'm finding it slow to evaluate, yielding only 1000-2000 effective samples after a day of crunching on a relatively fast machine. While this is ok for now, I was hoping on increasing the complexity to the model, including adding parameters to evaluate correlations across levels of my random effect amongst the existing parameters. Any advice on tweaks I might apply to make the code more efficient?

Oh, and in case this is related, I'm getting really strong autocorrelation in the samples for most of the parameters, even with chains of length 1e5. There's also pretty strong crosscorrelation between a few pairs of parameters.

Thoughts?

Well, for one you can vectorize things a bit more.  Instead of:

//define sampling of unit-specific parameters
for (n in 1:N){
logitRho[n] ~ normal(logitRhoMean,logitRhoSD);
logKappa[n] ~ normal(logKappaMean,logKappaSD);
logitRhoEffect[n] ~ normal(logitRhoEffectMean,logitRhoEffectSD);
logKappaEffect[n] ~ normal(logKappaEffectMean,logKappaEffectSD);
}

just do

logitRho ~ normal(logitRhoMean,logitRhoSD);
logKappa ~ normal(logKappaMean,logKappaSD);
logitRhoEffect ~ normal(logitRhoEffectMean,logitRhoEffectSD);
logKappaEffect ~ normal(logKappaEffectMean,logKappaEffectSD);

This will help a little, depending on how large N is.

Also, you should be able to compute log(rho[]) directly from logitRho.

Finally, if 2*N << L, then it might be worth precomputing values and just indexing them when looping over L.

Those things should help speed up the model, but won't necessarily help with convergence issues and strong autocorrelations.
